# Implement block: Orbit Photo Ring (React Native)

You are adding the "Orbit Photo Ring" block from Native Cook to the user's React Native app. The block already exists as working code. Your job is to bring it into this project faithfully, not to write a new one that looks similar.

## The block

A retro camera hangs in the dark, drawn in true perspective: a body in pebbled leather between chrome plates, a prism hump with knobs on top and a deep ribbed lens with tinted glass. Ten polaroid prints (white cards with a slightly tall photo, a pencil caption and a small ring mark) orbit it, the ones behind the camera smaller, darker and blurred. A switcher at the top offers three ring styles that morph into each other: Ring, a wide tilted halo around the camera at rest; Tumble, where the camera becomes a soft, glossy toy-like body ray-marched in 3D (a lacquered shell with a carry hump and two dark knobs over a satin body with a pale base, a deep knurled lens holding a matte white sphere, an accent dot and a small tab) that turns round together with a wide ring of polaroids, the front of both travelling left to right; the ring hangs low and is rolled so its left side sits lower than its right, its front prints sweeping across the lens and its back ones passing small under the body, every print leaning with it; and Gyro, two crossed rings of five spinning against each other. Under the scene sit the model's name and a line of specs, and at the bottom a bar of camera thumbnails that scrolls freely, the chosen one in colour: scrolling only browses, tapping a thumbnail chooses it. Dragging sideways spins the prints and turns the camera with them; choosing another camera spins the body as it morphs into the new model while the prints fly off and new ones are shot out of the lens.

**Motion.** The scene is a pinhole camera with a 700 pt focal length looking at the body 700 pt away (on a 402 pt wide screen, scaled to the real width); the body rests turned 28° and tipped 15° towards the viewer, every face drawn through its own perspective matrix and lit from the upper left, with the lens built from slices of a cylinder. Each ring style is a vector of numbers — ring radius, drop below the body, tilt, roll, print width, how far prints turn to the outside, body scale, tumble and split — and choosing a style (selection haptic; the light pill slides on a spring, 380 ms, damping ratio 0.86) morphs every number from wherever it is over 0.9 s on an ease-in-out curve. Ring: radius 206 pt, 14 pt drop, 21° tilt, −9° roll, 74 pt prints turning up to 28°. Tumble: radius 200, 155 pt drop, −20° tilt (the front edge raised), −16° roll, 76 pt prints turning 40° and leaning with the roll (1.15 times it, keeping a quarter of their own angles), back prints darkening and blurring less, the body 18% larger and facing the viewer 20° more squarely, and the whole scene 72 pt higher; a print passes behind the body once it is beyond the body's front face (80% of its half depth) rather than its middle, so the prints coming round the sides slip behind its edges; the box camera cross-fades into the toy camera with the style morph. The toy is one runtime shader (Skia in React Native, Metal in SwiftUI, AGSL in Jetpack Compose) that ray-marches signed distance fields (rounded boxes, a tapered hump with a slot, ribbed cylinders, spheres; up to 96 steps inside a bounding sphere, 0.75 pt soft silhouette, four-tap ambient occlusion) through the scene's own pinhole camera, lit by a key light from the upper left and front, a fill from the right and a studio of a softbox above and a strip on the left, so the shell reads as lacquered metal, the body as satin, the lens as rubber and the sphere as matte. Below Android 13, which has no runtime shaders, the Compose version keeps the box camera instead, its metal and leather taking the toy's shell and body colours, and tumbles it the same way. In Tumble the ring rests instead of idling and makes one whole turn twice a loop on an ease-in-out curve (0.4–4.2 s and 9.7–12.5 s, between the camera changes), and the body turns round with it about an axis leaning back and to the side, so halfway round it shows its base; both fronts travel left to right, and a camera change spins the body the same way. Dragging the ring turns the body with it, and after a release the body comes back round to face the viewer (rate 2.6/s). The body sways ±5° four times a loop; a whole turn ends where it began, so the loop is seamless, and while the style morphs the turn is scaled the short way round. Gyro: radius 188, 6 pt drop, 64° tilt, prints 66 pt turning 18°, the body at 88%; the odd prints form a second ring and the two rings roll ±34° and spin against each other, the second always the mirror image of the first. Prints are 100 × 126 units with an 88 × 98 photo; they float 4 pt twice a loop and, behind the body, darken up to 62% and blur up to 3.2 px with depth. Idle, the ring spins at about 0.33 rad/s. Dragging turns it with the finger at the speed of the front prints; a release throws it at the finger's speed (capped at 12 rad/s) and it coasts back to the idle spin with a 0.7 s time constant, with a light haptic for a throw faster than 2 rad/s. The body turns up to 26° with the ring's spin (tanh of the spin over 2.4 rad/s) and a vertical drag tilts body and ring on a rubber band (0.11° per pt), both on springs (stiffness 90, damping 11). Choosing a camera (medium haptic) spins the body one full turn in 1.1 s on an ease-in-out curve, morphing its proportions and colours into the next model between 30% and 70% of the turn while it dips to 86% and rises 18 pt; the prints fly out and down over 0.42 s, 25 ms apart, and the new ones are shot from the lens to their places over 0.75 s, 70 ms apart, starting 0.35 s in, growing with a slight overshoot; the name rolls letter by letter, 45 ms apart, and the bar slides the chosen camera to the middle on a spring (stiffness 200, damping 24). A drag that starts within 44 pt of the bar's middle line scrolls the bar instead of the ring, rubber-banding up to 0.45 cameras past either end; a flick coasts on with a 0.33 s time constant (capped at 30 cameras/s) and stops wherever it runs out, springing back at the ends. Scrolling never chooses a camera, only a tap does, and the highlight stays on the chosen one. Tapping the body fires the shutter: the glass flashes for 0.45 s and the body jumps back 3.5% (rigid haptic). autoPlay plays a 16 s LOOP from rest in the chosen style: a flick at 1.8 s, camera changes at 4.6, 8.2 and 12.6 s (to the next, the one after, and back), and a backward flick at 10.4 s, the idle spin set so the loop adds up to one whole turn (in Tumble the two turns take the place of the flicks and the idle spin). A touch pauses it for 3.5 s. Under reduced motion the ring does not idle or coast, the body does not spin, dip, tumble or turn with the ring (the toy camera still shows in Tumble, standing still), and the prints fade instead of flying.

## Reference source

The block is built and running in the Native Cook source repository. Each link below is a file on GitHub. To read one as plain text, replace `https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/` with `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/` in its address.

### Demo (start here)

- [index.tsx](https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/main/react-native/src/blocks/media/orbit-photo-ring/index.tsx)

### Files of the block

- [OrbitPhotoRing.tsx](https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/main/react-native/src/blocks/media/orbit-photo-ring/OrbitPhotoRing.tsx)
- [OrbitPhotoRingToy.ts](https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/main/react-native/src/blocks/media/orbit-photo-ring/OrbitPhotoRingToy.ts)

### Packages

- `expo-haptics`
- `expo-status-bar`
- `react-native-gesture-handler`
- `react-native-reanimated`
- `react-native-safe-area-context`
- `@shopify/react-native-skia`
- `react-native-worklets`

The versions the block was built with are in [react-native/package.json](https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/main/react-native/package.json).

## Your instructions

_Anything specific to this app goes here: where the block should appear, what to rename, what to change. Left empty, integrate the block as it is._

## How to work

Work like an experienced React Native engineer joining an existing project: learn the app first, read only what you need, decide early how the block fits, then integrate it with as little disruption as possible. Take the steps in order.

**Done means** the block is reachable in the user's app and behaves like the reference on iOS or Android: a simulator, an emulator or a device. A browser is never proof. Do not open the app on the web to check it, not even when the mobile build fails.

**Fidelity.** Bring over the real implementation. Keep its structure, colours, sizes, timings and easing. Change only what this project requires and what "Your instructions" ask for.

If you already learned this project earlier in the conversation, reuse what you know and skip step 2. Learn it again only if the project changed or something you need is missing.

### 1. Check where you are

- You need the project's files and a terminal. If this prompt was pasted into a chat that has neither, stop and say so: it has to be run by a coding agent opened on the project.
- Confirm the project is a React Native app, Expo or bare. If it is something else, stop, say what you found, and do not create a new app inside it unless the instructions ask for one.

### 2. Learn the host app

- Expo (managed or prebuild) or bare React Native, and the versions of React Native and the Expo SDK.
- The package manager, and how the app is started: Expo Go, a development build, or `react-native run-ios` / `run-android`.
- Navigation: Expo Router, React Navigation, something else, or a single screen. Find how a screen is added today.
- Conventions: TypeScript or not, path aliases, how styles are written, where components and screens live.
- Which of the block's packages are already installed, and at which versions.

### 3. Read the block

- Open the demo, then each file it imports. The list above names every file of the block, so you do not have to guess.
- The demo is how the source repository shows the block. Bring over what the demo renders, not the repository's gallery. Anything listed under "Used by the demo only" stays behind.
- Read the block's props and their defaults. The demo may switch on an option that makes the block play by itself for a recording (for example `autoPlay`). Keep the option; leave it off in the user's app unless asked.

### 4. Decide the fit

- Compare the block's packages with the host's. Install what is missing with the project's own tool (`npx expo install …` in an Expo app, so versions match its SDK).
- A package with native code needs a new native build, and Expo Go only runs the modules it ships with. Say so before you install one, and say which build the user will need.
- If the host is on older versions and an API differs, adapt the block's code to the host. Do not upgrade the host's React Native, Expo SDK or animation libraries without asking.
- Put the files where this app keeps its components. Ask only when two places are equally reasonable and the choice matters.

### 5. Bring it in

- Copy the block's files, keep their names, and rewrite imports to this project's paths and aliases.
- Copy its images and fonts with it, and load fonts the way the project already does.
- Keep reduced-motion handling, haptics and accessibility labels as they are in the source.
- Mount the block where the instructions say. With no instructions, add a screen or route named after the block and make it reachable the way the app's other screens are.

### 6. Run it

- Typecheck and lint with the project's own commands and fix what the block introduced.
- Run the app on the user's usual mobile target and use the block: every state, every gesture, and once with reduced motion on.
- If the simulator, the emulator or the native build fails, report the error and ask how to continue. Do not fall back to the web.

### 7. Report

- Files added and changed, packages installed, and whether a new native build is needed.
- How to reach the block in the app.
- Anything that differs from the reference, and why.
